idea.body: A solid's volume is how much space it fills, in cubic units. A prism's or cylinder's volume is its base area times its height. A cone holds a third of the cylinder that fits snugly around it, and a pyramid holds a third of its matching prism. Three copies of the pointed solid exactly fill the straight one. A sphere's volume is 4 thirds of pi times its radius cubed. Cavalieri's idea says two solids with the same cross-section area at every height have the same volume, even if one is tilted or oblique.

figure.alt: A cone, radius 6 and height 9 centimeters.

workedExample.prompt: A 3D printer's storage cone has radius 6 centimeters and height 9 centimeters. Find its volume, as a multiple of pi.
steps: A cone's volume is a third of pi times radius squared times height.
36 times 9 is 324, and a third of 324 is 108.
The volume is 108 pi cubic centimeters.

figure.alt: A cone, radius 6 and height 9 centimeters.

ways.name: Base area times height
ways.when: Use this for a prism or cylinder: find the base's area, then multiply by the height.
steps: A cylinder has radius 4 centimeters and height 7 centimeters.
The base is a circle of radius 4, with area pi times 4 squared, which is 16 pi.
Multiply the base area by the height: 16 pi times 7 is 112 pi.
ways.example: A cylinder has radius 4 centimeters and height 7 centimeters. Find its volume, as a multiple of pi.
ways.trap: Using the diameter instead of the radius when squaring the base.

figure.alt: A cylinder, radius 4 and height 7 centimeters.

ways.name: The third of the matching solid
ways.when: Use this for a cone or pyramid: find the matching prism or cylinder's volume, then take a third.
steps: A square pyramid has a base 6 by 6 centimeters and height 8 centimeters.
The matching prism would have volume equal to base area times height: 6 times 6 times 8 is 288.
The pyramid holds exactly a third of that prism's volume.
ways.example: A square pyramid has a base 6 by 6 centimeters and height 8 centimeters. Find its volume.
ways.trap: Forgetting to divide by three and giving the full prism's volume instead.

figure.alt: A square pyramid, base 6 by 6 and height 8 centimeters.

ways.name: Count unit cubes
ways.when: Use this for a prism with whole-number sides, to see volume as a stack of unit cubes.
steps: A prism is 4 units long, 2 units wide, and 2 units tall.
The front face is a 4 by 2 grid of unit cubes, which is 8 cubes.
There are 2 layers front to back, so stack another 8 cubes behind.
Count all the cubes: 8 plus 8 is 16.
ways.example: A prism is 4 units long, 2 units wide, and 2 units tall. Find its volume in cubic units.
ways.trap: Counting only the front layer of cubes and forgetting the layer behind it.

figure.alt: A prism 4 units long, 2 units wide and 2 units tall, shown as one front layer of unit cubes.

ways.name: Cavalieri's idea
ways.when: Use this to compare a tilted or oblique solid to a straight one with the same base and height.
steps: A right prism has a square base of side 5 centimeters and height 9 centimeters.
An oblique prism leans sideways but has the same square base and the same straight-up height.
Cavalieri's idea says two solids with the same cross-section area at every height have the same volume.
The oblique prism's volume matches the right prism's: 25 times 9 = 225.
ways.example: A right prism has a square base of side 5 centimeters and height 9 centimeters. An oblique prism has the same base and the same straight-up height. Find the oblique prism's volume.
ways.trap: Measuring the slanted side length instead of the straight-up height.
